nameStory: Yellow foxglove gets its name from the bright golden-yellow color of its trumpet-shaped flowers, combined with the old folk belief that foxes slipped the blooms over their paws like gloves to muffle their steps while hunting. The 'grandiflora' part of its scientific name means 'large-flowered,' highlighting how these sunny blooms are bigger and showier than many of its foxglove cousins.
description: Yellow foxglove is a tall, stately perennial that can reach 2-4 feet high, creating impressive spikes of large, pale yellow trumpet-shaped flowers. Each bloom is about 1-2 inches long and hangs downward from sturdy stems, giving the whole plant a dramatic, architectural look. The soft, fuzzy leaves form a basal rosette at the bottom, with smaller leaves climbing up the flowering stem. Originally from southern Europe and Asia, this striking plant has found its way into New England gardens and occasionally escapes into the wild.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large, pale yellow trumpet-shaped blooms hang downward in tall spikes, each flower 1-2 inches long with a slightly inflated, tubular shape and subtle brown veining inside the throat

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Soft, fuzzy leaves that feel almost woolly to the touch, arranged in a rosette at the base with lance-shaped leaves getting smaller as they climb the stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, upright perennial reaching 2-4 feet with a single or few sturdy flowering stems rising from a leafy base, creating a bold vertical presence

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, egg-shaped capsules develop after flowering, splitting open to release tiny brown seeds that feel like fine dust when rubbed between fingers

habitat: In New England, yellow foxglove is primarily found in cultivated gardens but occasionally escapes to naturalize along woodland edges, disturbed slopes, and areas with well-drained soil. It prefers partial shade to full sun and thrives in spots that mimic its native mountain habitat - warm, somewhat protected areas with good drainage.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge from the base in a soft, fuzzy rosette, and flower stalks begin to develop in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from early to mid-summer, with the spectacular yellow flower spikes lasting several weeks and attracting bees and other pollinators.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules mature and split open, while the basal leaves may persist as flowering stems die back.
seasonality.winter: Plants go dormant with only dead stems remaining above ground, though the root system survives to regrow next spring.

funFact: Despite its beautiful appearance, yellow foxglove contains the same heart-affecting compounds (digitalis) that have been used in heart medications for over 200 years - making it both a garden treasure and a plant to admire from a safe distance, especially around children and pets.
confusionNotes: Yellow foxglove might be confused with mullein when not in bloom, but mullein leaves are much larger, thicker, and more densely woolly, feeling almost like flannel. Once flowering, the distinctive downward-hanging trumpet blooms of foxglove are unmistakable compared to mullein's small yellow flowers clustered tightly on the stem.
contextualKnowledge: All foxgloves contain cardiac glycosides and should never be ingested - they're the source of the heart medication digitalis, but are highly toxic when consumed. Always teach children to look but never touch or taste any foxglove species, despite their garden-friendly appearance.
compareHints: Yellow foxglove stands out from its more common cousin, purple foxglove, by its soft yellow color and larger individual blooms. While purple foxglove has deep magenta-purple flowers with spotted throats, yellow foxglove's blooms are pale yellow with subtle brown veining. Straw foxglove has much smaller, narrower pale yellow flowers, making yellow foxglove the showiest of the yellow-flowered foxgloves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Purple foxglove is the most common foxglove species in New England and the most likely to naturalize from gardens.

Among foxgloves in New England, straw foxglove is distinguished by its pale, cream-yellow flowers that are much smaller and more numerous than the large, bright yellow blooms of yellow foxglove (Digitalis grandiflora).
Woolly foxglove stands out from other foxgloves by its distinctly fuzzy, grayish leaves and small, densely-packed cream flowers.
Among the foxglove family, Rusty Foxglove is unique for its rust-brown flowers - Purple Foxglove has pink-purple blooms, while Yellow Foxglove (rarely seen here) has pale yellow flowers.
